valuation.net_debt_note: EV = market cap + latest borrowings. Screener's public page does not split cash out of other assets, so cash is not netted off; investments are shown separately.

dcf.method: 5-year FCFF: EBITDA - tax on EBIT - capex - change in net working capital; growth fades linearly from the starting rate to the year-5 rate; Gordon terminal value; equity = EV - borrowings.

inputs.growth_basis: median of 3-year, 5-year and TTM sales growth, capped 0-30%
inputs.capex_rule: depreciation + new sales / fixed-asset turnover (median of the last three years)

reverse_dcf.note: Constant sales growth for five years, at the base margin and the same WACC and terminal growth, that makes the DCF equal today's EV.

blocks.text: Millworks Technologies Limited is a precision engineering manufacturer that makes precision-machined components, sheet-metal parts and integrated assemblies for what it describes as mission-critical applications in Defence, Railways, Aerospace and Semiconductor industries [F] (SCREENER). It was incorporated in November 2021 [F] (SCREENER) and is classified under Industrials > Capital Goods > Aerospace & Defense [F] (SCREENER). The company earns revenue by manufacturing parts and assemblies to customer drawings and selling them per piece or per assembly [AI] (SCREENER); whether it is a build-to-print job shop, a design-and-build supplier or both is not established by our evidence, although the profile says it specialises in 'design, development, and production' [MC] (SCREENER).

**The evidence base is unusually thin.** For this initiation we had our statements data (five fiscal years FY22-FY26, standalone, no quarterly data), a two-paragraph company profile, five exchange announcements from September 2026 and our own earlier research notes. No annual report, no offer document (DRHP/RHP/prospectus), no earnings-call transcript and no investor presentation were available [F] (NUMBERS, SCREENER, ANNOUNCEMENTS). Consequently end-market split, geography split, customer names, concentration, order book, capacity and management identities are all **not disclosed** in our evidence, and this is itself a central finding [AI].

subsections.title: Listing status and what it means for the evidence base

blocks.text: Our earlier research notes record an IPO at Rs 331 per share with listing on 21 July 2026 on what they describe as an SME-series BSE code [F] (BOARD); we could not verify these facts against an offer document, which was not available [AI]. Shareholding data begins only in July 2026 (promoters 47.18%, FIIs 2.55%, DIIs 10.28%, public 39.98%, 2,687 shareholders) [F] (NUMBERS), so there is no holding trend. Our data contains no quarterly results [F] (NUMBERS); if the listing is on the SME platform, results would be half-yearly [AI]. The trading window was closed from 27 September 2026 [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS), consistent with results for the period ending 30 September 2026 being prepared [AI]. The company published notice of its 5th annual general meeting on 8 September 2026 [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS), consistent with a November 2021 incorporation [AI].

Every conclusion in this report rests on five years of rounded, standalone screener.in figures, the last four of which are pre-listing. With no audited annual report or offer document, we cannot test revenue recognition, related-party dealings, customer identity or auditor commentary. Treat all positive signals as provisional [AI].

subsections.title: Bear thesis: reasons not to own it

items: 1. **Profits are not converting to cash.** FY26 PAT Rs 37 cr against operating cash flow of -Rs 11 cr; three-year CFO/PAT -0.3x and three-year free cash flow -Rs 33 cr [F] (NUMBERS).

2. **Receivables of 340 days.** Debtor days rose from 112 in FY25 to 340 in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS), implying roughly Rs 139 cr of receivables against Rs 149 cr of revenue [E] (NUMBERS) - most of the year's sales were uncollected at year-end, consistent with heavily year-end-loaded billing [AI].
3. **Pre-IPO growth spike.** Revenue rose about 577% and PAT about 640% in FY26, the year before listing [E] (NUMBERS); nothing in our evidence explains which customers or orders drove it [AI].

4. **Price sits far above every DCF scenario.** Rs 1,208 versus bear/base/bull values of Rs 194/341/485, i.e. -83.9%/-71.8%/-59.9% [F] (NUMBERS); the reverse DCF needs 60.3% sales growth for five years versus a 19.8% base-case equivalent [F] (NUMBERS).

5. **Supplier credit of 349 days funds the model.** Payable days 349 and other liabilities up from Rs 7 cr to Rs 99 cr in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS); the counterparties and terms are undisclosed, and the low headline cash cycle of 47 days depends on them [AI].
6. **Evidence vacuum.** No annual report, offer document, transcript, segment data, customer list or order book in our evidence [AI]; the investment case cannot be audited from outside.
7. **Very young operating history.** Incorporated November 2021 [F] (SCREENER); FY23 revenue was Rs 2 cr [F] (NUMBERS). There is no through-cycle record.

8. **Unexplained equity movements.** Equity capital rose from Rs 0.06 cr to Rs 13 cr in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS); net worth rose about Rs 60 cr against PAT of Rs 37 cr, leaving about Rs 23 cr of capital inflow whose nature and pricing are not disclosed [E] (NUMBERS).
9. **Promoter holding below half, no trend.** Promoters held 47.18% in July 2026 and no prior data exists [F] (NUMBERS); lock-in expiries could add supply [AI].

10. **Thin, momentum-driven trading.** 2,687 shareholders [F] (NUMBERS); price roughly 3.6x the Rs 331 issue price recorded in our notes [E] (NUMBERS, BOARD); 52-week range Rs 629-1,306 [F] (NUMBERS).

Is FY26 a run-rate or a lump? Bull: a Rs 149 cr base at 35% margin is a new platform [AI]. Bear: 340 debtor days suggest a concentrated year-end billing event [AI] (NUMBERS). Neither side can prove it without H1 FY27 results.

Are 35% EBITDA margins a moat or a mix artefact? Mission-critical precision work can earn premium margins [AI] (SCREENER); but margins this high on a four-year-old job-shop-type asset base are unusual and untested by any customer or cost disclosure [AI].

Is the negative cash flow growth investment or a quality problem? Bull: working capital absorbs cash in a scale-up [AI]. Bear: CFO was negative in three of four reported years [F] (NUMBERS), including FY25 when growth was slower.
Does the market price an order book we cannot see? Possibly - the price requires 60.3% five-year growth [F] (NUMBERS) - but no order book is disclosed in our evidence [AI].
Is the post-IPO balance sheet much stronger than FY26 shows? Likely yes if the IPO had a fresh-issue component [AI]; proceeds and use of funds are not in our evidence.

blocks.text: The market appears to be pricing Millworks as a scarce listed indigenisation play whose FY26 profit is the start of a long compounding path [AI] (NUMBERS). Our variant view is that the one measurable piece of evidence that would distinguish a durable franchise from a pre-listing revenue event - cash collection - points the wrong way: FY26 receivables of about Rs 139 cr [E] and CFO of -Rs 11 cr [F] (NUMBERS). Until the company converts FY26 receivables into cash and shows H1 FY27 revenue that is not merely a continuation of year-end billing, we regard the FY26 margin and growth as unverified rather than proven [AI]. The counter-risk to our view is that a genuine qualified-supplier position with a defence or semiconductor-equipment anchor customer exists and simply has not been disclosed in the evidence available to us [AI].

**The current business is effectively one year old at scale.** 94% of cumulative FY23-FY26 revenue (Rs 149 cr of Rs 182 cr) was booked in FY26 [E] (NUMBERS). A company incorporated in November 2021 [F] (SCREENER) cannot have long approval histories with defence or aerospace primes in its own name unless it inherited them from a predecessor entity or its promoters [AI]; whether that is the case is not disclosed. The short gap between the revenue step-up (FY26) and listing (July 2026, per our notes) is a pattern that warrants caution [AI] (BOARD).

blocks.text: In precision contract manufacturing, value typically accrues to suppliers that hold qualification on critical parts and can deliver integrated assemblies rather than loose components [AI]. Millworks reports a 35% EBITDA margin in FY25 and FY26 [F] (NUMBERS), which, if genuine, implies it is capturing value at the assembly or qualified-part level rather than competing as a commodity machine shop [AI]. The expense base was Rs 97 cr in FY26 against Rs 149 cr of revenue [F] (NUMBERS); the split between materials, labour, subcontracting and overheads is not in our data, so we cannot confirm where the margin comes from [AI].

Net fixed assets were Rs 25 cr and CWIP Rs 2 cr at March 2026 [F] (NUMBERS), supporting Rs 149 cr of revenue, a fixed-asset turnover of 5.96x [F] (NUMBERS). That is high for an in-house precision machining operation, which raises the possibility that part of the work is subcontracted or that FY26 revenue included a high bought-out or pass-through content [AI]. Payable days of 349 [F] (NUMBERS) are consistent with large back-to-back supplier arrangements, but the documents do not confirm this [AI].

blocks.text: No product-level revenue, volumes, prices or part counts are disclosed [AI].

Sheet-metal parts and build-to-print machined components are generally commodity-like, won on price and delivery [AI]. Integrated assemblies and qualified flight- or defence-critical parts are differentiated by approvals and traceability [AI]. We cannot tell which mix produced FY26's Rs 149 cr [AI]; the reported 35% margin [F] (NUMBERS) would be more consistent with the differentiated end, but a single large assembly order with significant bought-out content could also produce it [AI].
Totals [F] (NUMBERS); growth [E] (NUMBERS). Segment margins are not disclosed [AI]. The company appears to operate as a single reportable segment in our data [AI].

Management's explanation of the FY26 step-up is not in our evidence: no call transcript, annual report or presentation was available [AI]. The 9 September 2026 webinar and 18 September 2026 meeting took place but their content is not disclosed beyond the statement that no UPSI was shared [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS). Our read: the order of listing in the profile (Defence first) [F] (SCREENER) and the sector classification [F] (SCREENER) hint at defence as the lead market, but that is an inference only [AI].

Defence and railways supply is usually order- or tender-driven; semiconductor-equipment parts are usually programme-driven with repeat schedules [AI]. Given the FY26 revenue jump and receivables build [F] (NUMBERS), we assume FY26 was predominantly order-driven until shown otherwise [AI].

Semiconductor-equipment supply chains are largely export-oriented, while defence and railways are domestic [AI]; the actual currency exposure, hedging policy and imported-input share are not disclosed [AI]. We found no tariff or trade-policy disclosures with dates [AI]. The number and location of plants are not disclosed; with net fixed assets of Rs 25 cr [F] (NUMBERS) a single-site operation is plausible, which would concentrate operational risk [AI].
No case studies, long-term agreements or purchase-order structures are disclosed in our evidence [AI].

It cannot be measured. Two indirect signals point to high concentration [AI]: (1) a Rs 127 cr revenue increase in one year [E] (NUMBERS) is typically driven by one or a few large orders in precision contract manufacturing [AI]; (2) receivables of roughly 340 days of sales [F] (NUMBERS) are more consistent with a few large invoices than a diversified base [AI]. The opposite reading - many new customers onboarded simultaneously - cannot be ruled out, and would be the bull interpretation [AI]. We present both because the data does not decide between them.

blocks.text: No client is named or identifiable from our evidence [AI]. For a company whose premium rests on being qualified for mission-critical programmes, the absence of any named customer, approval or programme in the evidence available to us is the single largest gap in the investment case [AI]. The offer document, if obtained, would likely contain the top-customer disclosures that are missing here [AI].

**No order book, backlog, L1 position or order inflow is disclosed in the evidence available to us** [AI]. We have no management statement on orders because no transcript or presentation was available [AI]. The profile's closing phrase in our notes - 'essentially unknown outside its own order book' - is an analyst remark, not a disclosure of an order book [F] (BOARD).

blocks.text: Only category A exists in our evidence. Any valuation above the base DCF of Rs 341 per share [F] (NUMBERS) must implicitly rely on categories B-E, none of which we can see [AI].

Defence is listed first in the business description and drives the Aerospace & Defense classification [F] (SCREENER). Position in the value chain: likely a tier-2/tier-3 supplier of machined parts and assemblies to primes or public-sector units [AI]; no programme, platform or customer is disclosed. Government exposure cannot be quantified [AI]. What exists today versus narrative: a production business with Rs 149 cr FY26 revenue [F] (NUMBERS); what share is defence is not disclosed [AI]. If defence customers are large public-sector units, the 340 debtor days [F] (NUMBERS) would be partly explained by their payment cycles, which would be a structural, not temporary, working-capital burden [AI].

Semiconductor is named as an end market [F] (SCREENER). Our earlier notes frame it as import substitution of precision assemblies previously made in the US, Europe or Taiwan [AI] (BOARD). Nothing disclosed indicates whether Millworks supplies global equipment makers, Indian fab projects or neither [AI]. This is the line with the most narrative and the least evidence [AI].

blocks.text: No installed capacity, machine count, shift pattern or utilisation figure is disclosed in the evidence available [AI]. An aggregate utilisation trend therefore cannot be shown.

All figures [F] (NUMBERS). FY25 shows capacity added ahead of revenue (turnover fell to 1.69x) and FY26 shows that capacity being filled (5.96x) [AI]. The FY26 jump in turnover is large for machining assets and could reflect higher utilisation, multi-shift working, subcontracting or bought-out content [AI]; the documents do not say which.

Sensitivity, not base case: if the FY26 fixed-asset turnover of 5.96x [F] (NUMBERS) were held on the March 2026 net block plus CWIP of Rs 27 cr, revenue capacity would be about Rs 161 cr [E] (NUMBERS), only slightly above FY26 revenue - implying further growth needs new capex or outsourcing [AI]. Whether the premises are owned or leased, and any lease expiries, are not disclosed [AI].
Capex, capex/revenue and CWIP [F] (NUMBERS); capex/EBITDA [E] (NUMBERS). Our earlier notes describe capex as small and flat, CWIP about 8% of net block [F] (BOARD); this agrees with our data [AI].

From FY24 to FY26 revenue rose Rs 140 cr while net fixed assets rose Rs 23 cr and cumulative capex was Rs 17 cr [E] (NUMBERS). On fixed capital alone that is exceptional capital efficiency [AI]. On total capital it is not: other assets (mainly receivables) rose Rs 158 cr from FY24 to FY26 [E] (NUMBERS). The growth has been working-capital-heavy rather than fixed-capital-heavy [AI].

No capex plan, IPO object of issue or funding mix is disclosed in our evidence [AI]. Our DCF model assumes capex equal to depreciation plus new sales divided by a 4.5x fixed-asset turnover [F] (NUMBERS). Classification: asset-light on fixed assets, capital-heavy on working capital [AI].

Key raw materials, their sources, import share by year and supplier countries are not disclosed [AI]. Precision parts for these end markets typically use aluminium alloys, steels, stainless and specialty alloys [AI], but we have no company evidence on mix. No price trend data is in the documents. Pass-through ability is not claimed or evidenced in our material [AI].

items: FY24 (30%): operating leverage off a Rs 2 cr base [AI]; temporary scale effect.

None of these can be checked without H1 FY27 data [AI].

No annual report or offer document was available to cross-check line items [AI].

subsections.title: Why TAM does not translate to revenue

blocks.text: With no TAM figure available we cannot even do illustrative share arithmetic [AI]. More importantly, a precision supplier's revenue is bounded by the number of qualified parts on programmes it has won, not by sector size [AI]. A bottom-up framing would require: named programmes x parts approved x annual volumes x realisation; none of these inputs is disclosed [AI]. The only bottom-up anchor is FY26 revenue of Rs 149 cr from a Rs 25 cr net block [F] (NUMBERS).

Demand in defence and railways in India is concentrated in a small number of government-owned buyers and primes, giving buyers strong bargaining power over pricing and payment timing [AI]. Semiconductor equipment demand is concentrated in a handful of global OEMs [AI]. Either way the supplier side is fragmented and the buyer side concentrated [AI].

The DCF uses a 15% WACC (effectively cost of equity), 5.5% terminal growth, and a 35% margin taken straight from FY26 [F] (NUMBERS). It is generous on working capital (76.3 days vs 111 actual) [F] (NUMBERS) and on margin persistence [AI]; it is conservative only in capping starting growth at 30% [F] (NUMBERS). The bear / base / bull values are 83.9% / 71.8% / 59.9% below the current price [F] (NUMBERS). The base DCF value of Rs 341 is close to the Rs 331 issue price recorded in our notes [F] (NUMBERS, BOARD).

At the base margin, WACC and terminal growth, today's EV requires **60.3% constant annual sales growth for five years**, against a base-case equivalent of 19.8% [F] (NUMBERS). That is above the bull case's first-year growth of 43.5% [F] (NUMBERS), sustained for five years. History shows 320.8% three-year CAGR [F] (NUMBERS), but off a Rs 2 cr base that is not a meaningful anchor [AI].

The market is capitalising FY26 accrual profit as if it were high-quality, repeatable and cash-generative, when FY26 CFO was negative and receivables equalled about 340 days of sales [F] (NUMBERS). The price requires growth beyond our bull case on a revenue base whose durability is unproven [AI].

If Millworks has in fact secured multi-year qualified positions on defence or semiconductor programmes - not disclosed in our evidence but possible - then the FY26 step-up could be the first year of a much larger ramp, working capital would normalise as billing smooths out, and a high-growth multiple could be justified [AI]. DII ownership of 10.28% shortly after listing [F] (NUMBERS) suggests some institutions had access to information (for example the offer document) that we did not [AI].

blocks.text: All figures [F] (NUMBERS).

Our model's year-5 sales range spans Rs 223.8 cr (bear) to Rs 507.9 cr (bull) [F] (NUMBERS). Outcomes outside that range in both directions are plausible for a company this young: a failure to repeat FY26 would put revenue below the bear path, while programme wins could exceed the bull path [AI]. The price is currently consistent only with the upper tail [AI] (NUMBERS).

At Rs 1,208 the share price sits well above every scenario in our DCF model - bear Rs 194, base Rs 341, bull Rs 485 [F] (NUMBERS) - and above every cell of the sensitivity grid [F] (NUMBERS). The gap is driven by the market extrapolating one year of rapid, high-margin growth; our model extrapolates it more cautiously and penalises nothing for cash conversion beyond the working-capital assumption [AI]. **The evidence we have does not support the growth the price requires, and the evidence we lack is exactly what would be needed to support it** [AI]. This is a view on evidence, not a rating.

summary.one_line: Millworks reported a pre-listing jump to Rs 149 cr revenue at a 35% EBITDA margin, but negative operating cash flow, 340 debtor days and near-total non-disclosure of customers and orders leave that profit unverified, while the Rs 1,208 price sits well above even the bull DCF value of Rs 485 and implies 60.3% annual growth for five years.
